Think about size - why would a very small DNA molecule be easier to move into a new cell and work with in a test tube?
For cloning, you need to open the plasmid and put a new gene in - what special DNA sequence must it contain to allow this cutting?
After you have mixed plasmids and bacteria, most bacteria will not have taken one up - what extra genes could help you spot the few that have?
Link that marker idea to its use - how does antibiotic resistance let you identify only transformed recombinant cells?

walkthrough:
What A Plasmid Is Built Like**
A plasmid is a small extra piece of double-stranded DNA found in bacteria, separate from the main chromosome. It is circular, which makes it stable and less easily broken down by enzymes inside the cell.

Getting The Gene In And The Plasmid In**
Being small helps the plasmid easily enter a host cell during transformation and is easy to manipulate. It has specific restriction sites where a restriction enzyme can cut it open, so the target gene can be inserted at exactly the right place.

Finding The Transformed Cells**
Plasmids carry marker genes, typically genes for antibiotic resistance. Only bacteria that have taken up the plasmid will survive on antibiotic plates, so you can identify the GM / transformed cells very quickly.

Making Many Copies Fast**
Once inside, the plasmid replicates independently of the host chromosome and very rapidly. That means every time the bacterium divides, the plasmid is copied too, giving many copies of the cloned gene for protein production or further use.

Final answer: Plasmids are small, circular, double-stranded DNA. They contain restriction sites / target sequences for restriction enzymes allowing the gene for cloning to be inserted. They can enter / transform host bacterial cells. They contain marker genes for antibiotic resistance used to identify transformed / recombinant cells. They replicate rapidly and independently of host replication to give many copies of the cloned gene, and are stable.

hints: Split the three enzymes in your mind - one cuts, one joins, and one copies RNA into DNA. Which one do you think acts first on the plasmid and the donor DNA?
For the cutting enzyme, think about precision - does it cut anywhere, or only at a very specific base sequence?
Recall the word palindrome in DNA - why does cutting at such a sequence naturally leave ends that can match up again?
Think about the result of cutting - what are sticky ends and blunt ends, and why are sticky ends especially useful for joining?
Now move to the joining enzyme - once the gene and opened plasmid are lined up, what backbone needs to be sealed?
Name the bond that must be re-made to create a continuous recombinant plasmid, and what the final product is called.
For the third enzyme, think backwards from its name - if transcription is DNA to mRNA, what template and product does reverse transcriptase use?
Consider why this is useful - why would starting from mRNA give you a clean gene copy without introns, and what is the first strand like?
walkthrough:
Restriction Endonucleases - Precise Molecular Scissors**
These enzymes cut DNA only at specific target sequences called restriction sites, which are often palindromes - the same sequence reads forwards and backwards. Cutting there opens both the plasmid and the donor DNA and leaves sticky ends with unpaired bases or blunt ends.

Ligases - Molecular Glue**
After the target gene has base-paired with the opened plasmid via complementary sticky ends, ligase joins them together. It seals the sugar-phosphate backbone on both strands by making new covalent phosphodiester bonds.

Making Recombinant DNA**
The result of cutting with the same restriction enzyme and then ligating is a single continuous molecule: recombinant DNA / recombinant plasmid. That plasmid now carries the foreign gene and can be put back into bacteria.

Reverse Transcriptase - From mRNA Back To DNA**
This enzyme uses mRNA as a template to synthesise a complementary single strand of DNA, called cDNA. This is very useful because mRNA has already been spliced, so the cDNA contains only exons with no introns, giving a clean coding sequence ready to be made double-stranded, cut and ligated into a vector.

Final answer: Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at restriction / specific palindromic base sequences to give sticky / blunt ends. Ligases join the gene to the plasmid / vector by sealing the sugar-phosphate backbone, forming phosphodiester / covalent bonds to make recombinant DNA / plasmid. Reverse transcriptase makes single-stranded cDNA from an mRNA template.
